--- title: Cholesky Factorization --- ## Packages ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using LinearAlgebra, Random using Distributions using BenchmarkTools ``` ::: ## Cholesky decomposition In the normal equations for linear regression $$ \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \beta = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}, $$ the coefficient matrix $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite. **How to exploit this structure?** **Theorem**: Let $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be symmetric and positive definite. Then $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{L}^T$, where $\mathbf{L}$ is lower triangular with positive diagonal entries and is unique. ::: {.callout-note} **Positive definite**: - Eigenvalues of $\mathbf{A}$ are all positive - The quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} > 0$. - The matrix $\mathbf{A}$ defines an inner product. ::: **Proof** (by induction): If $n=1$, then $\ell = \sqrt{a}$. For $n>1$, the block equation \begin{eqnarray*} \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & \mathbf{a}^T \\ \mathbf{a} & \mathbf{A}_{22} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \ell_{11} & \mathbf{0}_{n-1}^T \\ \mathbf{l} & \mathbf{L}_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \ell_{11} & \mathbf{l}^T \\ \mathbf{0}_{n-1} & \mathbf{L}_{22}^T \end{pmatrix} \end{eqnarray*} has solution \begin{eqnarray*} \ell_{11} &=& \sqrt{a_{11}} \\ \mathbf{l} &=& \ell_{11}^{-1} \mathbf{a} \\ \mathbf{L}_{22} \mathbf{L}_{22}^T &=& \mathbf{A}_{22} - \mathbf{l} \mathbf{l}^T = \mathbf{A}_{22} - a_{11}^{-1} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{a}^T. \end{eqnarray*} Now $a_{11}>0$ (why?), so $\ell_{11}$ and $\mathbf{l}$ are uniquely determined. $\mathbf{A}_{22} - a_{11}^{-1} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{a}^T$ is positive definite because $\mathbf{A}$ is positive definite (why?). By induction hypothesis, $\mathbf{L}_{22}$ exists and is unique. ::: {.callout-note} The [Sherman-Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman%E2%80%93Morrison_formula) formula, [Woodbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbury_matrix_identity) formula, and [Schur complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schur_complement) are useful in - proving certain structured matrices are invertible, and - reducing the complexity of solving certain linear systems. ::: The constructive proof completely specifies the algorithm: ![](assets/cholesky.png){fig-align=center width=50%} ## Complexity $$ \frac{1}{2} [2(n-1)^2 + 2(n-2)^2 + \cdots + 2 \cdot 1^2] \approx \frac{1}{3} n^3 \quad \text{flops} $$ - Half the cost of LU decomposition by taking advantage of symmetry. - In general Cholesky decomposition is very stable. Failure of the decomposition usually means $\mathbf{A}$ is not positive definite. It is an efficient way to test positive definiteness. :::::::::::::::: callout-note Leading order behavior comes from cost of setting up $\mathbf{L}_{22}$ block in recursive application of the algorithm. :::::::::::::::: ## Applications **No inversion** mentality: Whenever we see matrix inverse, we should think in terms of solving linear equations. If the matrix is positive (semi)definite, use Cholesky decomposition, which is twice cheaper than LU decomposition. ### Determinant We should use Cholesky when computing $\operatorname{det}(\mathbf{A})$ or $\log \operatorname{det}(\mathbf{A})$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is positive definite. **Why?** ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} Random.seed!(206) Multivariate normal density Multivariate normal density $\text{MVN}(0, \Sigma)$, where $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}_{++}$ is postive definite, is $$ \, - \frac{n}{2} \log (2\pi) - \frac{1}{2} \log \det \Sigma - \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{y}^T \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{y}. $$ How can we evaluate this density? **Method 1**: (a) compute explicit inverse $\Sigma^{-1}$ ($2n^3$ flops), (b) compute quadratic form ($2n^2 + 2n$ flops), and finally (c) compute determinant ($2n^3/3$ flops). **Method 2**: (a) Cholesky decomposition $\Sigma = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{L}^T$ ($n^3/3$ flops), (b) Solve $\mathbf{L} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}$ by forward substitutions ($n^2$ flops), (c) compute quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}$ ($2n$ flops), and (d) compute determinant from Cholesky factor ($n$ flops). **Which method is better?** ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} # this is a person w/o numerical analysis training function logpdf_mvn_1(y::Vector, Σ::Matrix) n = length(y) - (n//2) * log(2π) - (1//2) * logdet(Symmetric(Σ)) - (1//2) * transpose(y) * inv(Σ) * y end # this is a computing-savvy person function logpdf_mvn_2(y::Vector, Σ::Matrix) n = length(y) Σchol = cholesky(Symmetric(Σ)) - (n//2) * log(2π) - (1//2) * logdet(Σchol) - (1//2) * abs2(norm(Σchol.L \ y)) end # better memory efficiency - input Σ is overwritten function logpdf_mvn_3(y::Vector, Σ::Matrix) n = length(y) Σchol = cholesky!(Symmetric(Σ)) # Σ is overwritten - (n//2) * log(2π) - (1//2) * logdet(Σchol) - (1//2) * dot(y, Σchol \ y) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` logpdf_mvn_3 (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#14 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} Random.seed!(206) # seed n = 1000 # a pd matrix Σ = convert(Matrix{Float64}, Symmetric([i * (n - j + 1) for i in 1:n, j in 1:n])) y = rand(MvNormal(Σ)) # one random sample from N(0, Σ) # at least they should give the same answer @show logpdf_mvn_1(y, Σ) @show logpdf_mvn_2(y, Σ) Σc = copy(Σ) @show logpdf_mvn_3(y, Σc); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` logpdf_mvn_1(y, Σ) = -4856.618941340982 logpdf_mvn_2(y, Σ) = -4856.618941341076 ``` ::: ::: ::: To evaluate the same multivariate normal density at many observations $y_1, y_2, \ldots$, we pre-compute the Cholesky decomposition ($n^3/3$ flops), then each evaluation only costs $n^2$ flops. ### Linear regression Cholesky decomposition is **one** approach to solve linear regression $$ \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}. $$ Assume $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ and $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n$. - Compute $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$: $np^2$ flops - Compute $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$: $2np$ flops - Cholesky decomposition of $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$: $\frac{1}{3} p^3$ flops - Solve normal equation $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} \beta = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$: $2p^2$ flops - If need standard errors, another $(4/3)p^3$ flops - Total computational cost is $np^2 + (1/3) p^3$ (without s.e.) or $np^2 + (5/3) p^3$ (with s.e.) flops.
